title: EXPLORING EFFECTS OF LIGHTING IN PHYSICAL AND VIRTUAL SPACES
research_question: Does the color temperature of electric lighting affect conflict handling behavior? And, what are the effects of virtual lighting (CCT and daylight) on perception and quality of stay in virtual spaces, and how transferable are measurement methods from physical to virtual spaces?

participants.description: Study CH1/CH2: N=68 each (55 males, 13 females; M=25.16, SD=2.60 years for CH1; 33 males, 35 females; M=25.16, SD=2.50 years for CH2), undergraduate/graduate psychology students at a German university. Normal/corrected-to-normal vision, normal color vision. Study VL1: N=95 (48 males, 47 females; M=29.79, SD=10.75 years), age 20-58, from 22 nationalities. Study VL2: N=106 (53 males, 53 females; M=21.17, SD=1.70 years), undergraduate business administration students, homogeneous nationality (104 German, 1 Italian, 1 French, raised/live in Germany).
participants.recruitment: Volunteered for partial course credit in psychology courses (CH1, CH2, VL2); social media and university campus (VL1).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Dimmable fluorescent ceiling lighting (4x Osram L18W 840) with filter foil (LEE 204 Full CTO) to change CCT. CH1: ~3,800 K (cold) vs. ~2,500 K (warm). CH2: ~1,600 K (reddish) vs. ~13,000 K (bluish). Illuminance constant at ~450 lx. Room: 12.5 m² with black walls and ceiling, no daylight.
Two conflict scenarios presented as text descriptions: landlord disagreement and uncooperative fellow student.
12 static renderings of virtual spaces (business applications). 6 pictures for warm (~2,300 K) / cold (~8,000 K) CCT lighting, 6 for virtual daylight / electric room lighting.

measures.construct: Emotional states (motivation, creativity, comfort, happiness, anxiousness)

measures.instrument: Slider scale (1,000 K to 14,000 K) for 13 situations

measures.construct: Perception and quality of stay in virtual spaces (Beauty, Brightness, Clutter, Glare, Hazy, Likeability, Pleasantness, Privacy, Relaxation, Stimulation, Specialty, Spaciousness, Visual temperature)
measures.instrument: Flynn's et al. (1979) semantic differential scale (13 items, 7-point Likert scale)

mechanisms: Conflict handling behavior is quite stable and not easily influenced by lighting conditions, but certain combinations of lighting condition, block order, and conflict case can affect specific styles (e.g., avoiding and accommodating).
Conceptual lighting (implicit expectations for lighting in a given environment) plays a role in influencing behavior, especially when lighting conditions are incongruent with expectations.
Limited cognitive resources for conflict resolution can lead to decreased accommodating behavior over time.
Higher light temperature (CCT) is associated with improved cognitive performance and is assigned to work-related situations based on biological expectations.
Virtual spaces are perceived as more spacious when presented in a cold white rather than warm white lighting scenario.
Virtual daylight is perceived as more beautiful, likeable, clearer, more spacious, brighter, more stimulating, and more ordinary than room lighting, consistent with a natural appraisal for daylight.
Cold white lighting is considered stimulating and tense and engenders a feeling of greater spaciousness.
The human visual system implicitly associates cold lighting with work-related spaces and warm lighting with private spaces through repeated exposure.

The observed weak tendency for higher happiness in bluish lighting conditions (CH2) can be explained by conceptual situational-lighting and space-lighting congruency, as university buildings typically use neutral to cold white illumination, aligning with student expectations.

The preference for virtual daylight and weather does not imply simulating local conditions, but rather using virtual spaces for positive experiences, differentiating them from the real environment to enhance immersion and experience.
moderators: Cultural background (influences privacy perception and CCT attribution to public/private domains)
Individual factors (e.g., genetic polymorphisms, biological sex, fatigue, hunger, emotional states)
implementation_implications: Lighting decisions in public spaces, trade fairs, congresses, and events should consider the welfare of guests, using bright, high CCT for alertness/concentration and dimmed, low CCT for relaxation.

Human-centered design for learning and working environments in virtual spaces should use virtual daylight to create impressions of larger spaces, addressing anxieties like claustrophobia and improving quality of stay.

In healthcare and nursing environments, HCL should create comfortable, home-like settings with warm, congruent lighting for calm/relaxation, while ensuring bright, cold white lighting for hygiene. Design should involve patients, caregivers, and professionals.
HCVL can optimize virtual spaces for dementia treatment (blue-enriched light for cognitive function/mood) and remote surgeries (stimulating light for concentration/accuracy).

Smart lighting systems in residential spaces should be adaptable to individual needs, changing CCT and intensity for different activities. Comparative cultural research is needed for appropriate lighting solutions.
HCVL can be used to create relaxing virtual atmospheres with warm white lighting.

Industrial lighting should prioritize work safety, ergonomics, and performance, with HCL considering circadian effects for shift work. Cool white lighting with high CCT is generally preferred for workplaces.

VR solutions in industrial sectors (training, design, prototyping) should incorporate realistic lighting, shadowing, and other features to enhance immersion and visual quality, based on HCVL insights.
In public and commercial virtual spaces, high CCT daylighting can increase perceived spaciousness, which is beneficial for confined spaces and can reduce anxiety for individuals with claustrophobia.

Virtual environments for entertainment, gaming, relaxation, and socialization should consider HCVL to optimize visual stimuli and enhance user experience. Virtual houses may incorporate windows with views to the virtual outside world.
Lighting dramaturgy can be integrated into virtual concerts and shows to enhance the overall experience.

limitations: Conflict style was recorded by self-assessment for imagined scenarios, not actual behavior, potentially limiting indication of actual expression.
Intercultural differences in lighting preferences and conflict management can mask lighting influences, requiring more cross-cultural studies for global validity.
Small effect sizes for psychological outcomes are challenging to detect, requiring higher sample sizes in future studies.
Practical limitations on laboratory study duration for ethical appropriateness and reasonableness towards participants.
Physiological measurements (e.g., heart rate, skin resistance) were not recorded in CH1/CH2, limiting examination of somatic effects.
Biotic environment of VL1 study includes uncontrollable confounding variables (e.g., external multisensory influences, prior light exposure).
Heterogeneity in technical specifications of devices used in VL1 (brightness, resolution, color rendering) could affect visual perception.
Static screenshots instead of movement in virtual environments in VL1/VL2 could influence subjective ratings.
Actual properties of daylight can only be reproduced to a very limited extent due to technical limitations of displays (brightness, spectral distribution).
Limited selection criteria in VL1 led to a heterogeneous sample (age, sex, nationality), potentially confounding effects.
VL2 study only included undergraduate students, limiting generalizability to the entire population.
Technical limitations of image rendering in HMDs can differ from screen-based representation, and movement through virtual spaces adds complexity.
Inter- and intrapersonal variables (fatigue, hunger, emotional states) could influence assessment in VL2.
Lack of standardized investigation approach and measurement instruments in lighting research limits comparability and quality of studies.
Glare sensation cannot be reproduced like real daylight due to lower luminous stimulus by HMDs.
VR glasses can cause motion sickness, which is an interfering variable.
Technological advancements mean new capabilities and virtual environments will require continuous further research.
